claim: Antigen recognition through the T cell receptor (TCR) αβ heterodimer is one of the primary determinants of the adaptive immune response.
source: Antigen recognition through the T cell receptor (TCR) αβ heterodimer is one of the primary determinants of the adaptive immune response.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Rudolph et al., 2006 in the introduction.

claim: Vaccines activate naïve T cells with high specificity to expand and differentiate into memory T cells.
source: Vaccines activate naïve T cells with high specificity to expand and differentiate into memory T cells.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about vaccine mechanisms.

claim: Antigen-specific memory CD4 T cells exist in unexposed antigen-naïve hosts.
source: However, antigen-specific memory CD4 T cells exist in unexposed antigen-naïve hosts.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Su et al., 2013 and Sewell, 2012 in the introduction.

claim: Individuals with preexisting vaccine-reactive memory CD4 T cell clonotypes elicited earlier antibody titers to hepatitis B vaccine.
source: In this study, we use high-throughput sequencing of memory CD4 TCRβ repertoire and machine learning to show that individuals with preexisting vaccine-reactive memory CD4 T cell clonotypes elicited earlier and higher antibody titers and mounted a more robust CD4 T cell response to hepatitis B vaccine.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript, including TCR sequencing and antibody titer measurements.

claim: Individuals with preexisting vaccine-reactive memory CD4 T cell clonotypes elicited higher antibody titers to hepatitis B vaccine.
source: In this study, we use high-throughput sequencing of memory CD4 TCRβ repertoire and machine learning to show that individuals with preexisting vaccine-reactive memory CD4 T cell clonotypes elicited earlier and higher antibody titers and mounted a more robust CD4 T cell response to hepatitis B vaccine.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript, including TCR sequencing and antibody titer measurements.

claim: Individuals with preexisting vaccine-reactive memory CD4 T cell clonotypes mounted a more robust CD4 T cell response to hepatitis B vaccine.
source: In this study, we use high-throughput sequencing of memory CD4 TCRβ repertoire and machine learning to show that individuals with preexisting vaccine-reactive memory CD4 T cell clonotypes elicited earlier and higher antibody titers and mounted a more robust CD4 T cell response to hepatitis B vaccine.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript, including TCR sequencing and CD4 T cell response measurements.

claim: Integration of TCRβ sequence patterns into a hepatitis B epitope-specific annotation model can predict which individuals will have an early and more vigorous vaccine-elicited immunity.
source: In addition, integration of TCRβ sequence patterns into a hepatitis B epitope-specific annotation model can predict which individuals will have an early and more vigorous vaccine-elicited immunity.
evidence: This claim is supported by the machine learning model results presented in the manuscript, including ROC curves showing predictive capacity.

claim: The presence of preexisting memory T cell clonotypes has a significant impact on immunity.
source: Thus, the presence of preexisting memory T cell clonotypes has a significant impact on immunity and can be used to predict immune responses to vaccination.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data showing differences in immune responses between individuals with and without preexisting memory T cell clonotypes.

claim: The presence of preexisting memory T cell clonotypes can be used to predict immune responses to vaccination.
source: Thus, the presence of preexisting memory T cell clonotypes has a significant impact on immunity and can be used to predict immune responses to vaccination.
evidence: This claim is supported by the predictive model results showing ability to distinguish early- from late-converters.

claim: The TCR αβ heterodimer binds the peptide-MHC (pMHC) complex and confers the specificity of a T cell to an epitope.
source: The TCR αβ heterodimer binds the peptide-MHC (pMHC) complex and confers the specificity of a T cell to an epitope.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about TCR function.

claim: High TCRαβ diversity is generated through V(D)J recombination at the complementary-determining region 3 (CDR3) of TCRα and TCRβ chains.
source: High TCRαβ diversity is generated through V(D)J recombination at the complementary-determining region 3 (CDR3) of TCRα and TCRβ chains, accompanied with junctional deletions and insertions of nucleotides, further adding to the diversity (Krangel, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Krangel, 2009.

claim: Out of 34 vaccinees, 21 vaccinees seroconverted at day 60 and were classified as early-converters.
source: Out of 34 vaccinees, 21 vaccinees seroconverted (an anti-HBs titer above 10 IU/ml was considered protective; Keating and Noble, 2003) at day 60 and were classified as early-converters
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Nine vaccinees seroconverted at day 180 or day 365 and were classified as late-converters.
source: nine vaccinees seroconverted at day 180 or day 365 and were classified as late-converters
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Four vaccinees had an anti-HBs antibody titer lower than 10 IU/ml at all time points following vaccination and were classified as non-converters.
source: remaining four vaccinees had an anti-HBs antibody titer lower than 10 IU/ml at all time points following vaccination and were classified as non-converters (Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: An anti-HBs titer above 10 IU/ml was considered protective.
source: an anti-HBs titer above 10 IU/ml was considered protective; Keating and Noble, 2003
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Keating and Noble, 2003.

claim: There were no significant differences in cytomegalovirus (CMV), Epstein-Barr virus (EBV), or herpes simplex virus (HSV) seropositivity between the three groups in the cohort.
source: We found no significant differences in cytomegalovirus (CMV), Epstein-Barr virus (EBV), or herpes simplex virus (HSV) seropositivity between the three groups in our cohort (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Early-converters were slightly younger than late-converters.
source: Early-converters were slightly younger than late-converters, and non-converters were notably younger than both early- and late-converters (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Non-converters were notably younger than both early- and late-converters.
source: Early-converters were slightly younger than late-converters, and non-converters were notably younger than both early- and late-converters (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Between 4.54 × 10^4 and 3.92 × 10^5 productive TCRβ sequence reads were obtained for each vaccinee at each time point.
source: Between 4.54 × 104 and 3.92 × 105 productive TCRβ sequence reads were obtained for each vaccinee at each time point (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Between 30,000 and 90,000 unique TCRβ sequences were sequenced for each vaccinee at each time point.
source: Between 30,000 and 90,000 unique TCRβ sequences were sequenced for each vaccinee at each time point (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Less than 20% of the TCRβ sequences is shared between the time points for each vaccinee.
source: As expected, considering the extremely diverse memory CD4 T cell repertoire (Klarenbeek et al., 2010), less than 20% of the TCRβ sequences is shared between the time points for each vaccinee (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and citation to Klarenbeek et al., 2010.

claim: Neither the breadth of the memory CD4 TCRβ repertoire nor the Shannon equitability index was found to have been impacted by the vaccine at day 60.
source: The diversity of the memory CD4 T cell repertoire of each vaccinee at the two time points was explored, but neither the breadth of the memory CD4 TCRβ repertoire nor the Shannon equitability index was found to have been impacted by the vaccine at day 60 (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: There was a significant increase in the breadth of HBsAg-specific TCRβ sequences at day 60 post-vaccination compared to pre-vaccination (mean increase = 107.9%, 95% CI = 62.2–358.5%).
source: We detected a significant increase in the breadth of HBsAg-specific TCRβ sequences at day 60 post-vaccination compared to pre-vaccination (mean increase = 107.9%, 95% CI = 62.2–358.5%) (Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The HBsAg-specific increase was found to be significant when compared to VZV baseline (Wilcoxon p-value 6.3e-05).
source: The HBsAg-specific increase was found to be significant when compared to this VZV baseline (Wilcoxon p-value 6.3e-05).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the data.

claim: The increase in HBsAg-specific TCRβ sequences was found to be significantly different from the VZV baseline for the early-converters (mean = 151.9%, 95% CI = 78.9–342.0%, Wilcoxon Bonferroni-corrected p-value 8.64e-5).
source: When considered across the different groups, the increase was found to be significantly different from the VZV baseline for the early-converters (mean = 151.9%, 95% CI = 78.9–342.0%, Wilcoxon Bonferroni-corrected p-value 8.64e-5)
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the data.

claim: The increase in HBsAg-specific TCRβ sequences was found to be significantly different from the VZV baseline for non-converters (mean = 67.6%, 95% CI: 37.6–89.7%, Wilcoxon Bonferroni-corrected p-value 0.03).
source: and non-converters (mean = 67.6%, 95% CI: 37.6–89.7%, Wilcoxon Bonferroni-corrected p-value 0.03)
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the data.

claim: The increase in HBsAg-specific TCRβ sequences was not significantly different from the VZV baseline for the late-converters (mean = 18.8%, 95% CI = 3.6–41.8%, Wilcoxon Bonferroni-corrected p-value 0.257).
source: but not for the late-converters (mean = 18.8%, 95% CI = 3.6–41.8%, Wilcoxon Bonferroni-corrected p-value 0.257).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the data.

claim: The data does not support a vaccine-induced expansion of preexisting vaccine-specific TCRβ sequences.
source: Based on the frequency of vaccine-specific TCRβ sequences within the memory CD4 T cell repertoire, the data does not support a vaccine-induced expansion of preexisting vaccine-specific TCRβ sequences (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E.

claim: The rise in vaccine-specific TCRβ T cells from day 0 to day 60 cannot be attributed to an expansion of the vaccine-specific TCRβ clonotypes found at day 0 but rather the recruitment of new TCRβ clonotypes.
source: Thus, although we see a rise in vaccine-specific TCRβ T cells from day 0 to day 60, this cannot be attributed to an expansion of the vaccine-specific TCRβ clonotypes found at day 0 but rather the recruitment of new TCRβ clonotypes, as visualized for one vaccinee in Figure 2C.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1E.

claim: There is a difference in HBsAg-specific TCRβ at day 60 between the three groups (ANOVA p-value = 0.00238).
source: From this analysis, it can be concluded that there is a difference in HBsAg-specific TCRβ at day 60 between the three groups (Figure 2D) (ANOVA p-value = 0.00238).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 2D and statistical analysis.

claim: Early-converters have a higher relative frequency of vaccine-specific TCRβ sequences present in their memory CD4 T cell repertoire at day 60 compared to vaccinees from the two other groups in the cohort (Wilcoxon test p-value = 0.000473).
source: A Wilcoxon test between early-converters and other vaccinees shows a significant p-value of 0.000473, indicating that early-converters have a higher relative frequency of vaccine-specific TCRβ sequences present in their memory CD4 T cell repertoire at day 60 compared to vaccinees from the two other groups in the cohort.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the data.

claim: Vaccine-specific TCRβ sequences increased in breadth following vaccination in early-converters.
source: In summary, vaccine-specific TCRβ sequences increased in breadth following vaccination in early-converters and constituted a significantly higher proportion of the memory CD4 T cell compartment post-vaccination.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data presented in Figure 2B and related analyses.

claim: Vaccine-specific TCRβ sequences constituted a significantly higher proportion of the memory CD4 T cell compartment post-vaccination in early-converters.
source: In summary, vaccine-specific TCRβ sequences increased in breadth following vaccination in early-converters and constituted a significantly higher proportion of the memory CD4 T cell compartment post-vaccination.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data presented in Figure 2D.

claim: TCRβ sequences were identified for T cells reactive against 44 single HBsAg peptides.
source: In this manner, TCRβ sequences were identified for T cells reactive against 44 single HBsAg peptides.
evidence: This claim is supported by the epitope mapping experiments described in the methods and results.

claim: The most prominent epitopes covering the regions 1–15, 129–144, 149–164, 161–176, 181–200, 213–228 had more than 10 individuals with a strong T cell response and more than 150 unique TCRβ sequences.
source: For each of those regions, more than 10 individuals had a strong T cell response and more than 150 unique TCRβ sequences could be identified (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The ratio Rhbs shows a significant difference between early- and the late-converters at day 60 (one-sided Wilcoxon-test p-value = 0.0313).
source: The ratio of these two terms Rhbs therefore shows a significant difference between early- and the late-converters at day 60 (one-sided Wilcoxon-test p-value = 0.0313, Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 3C and statistical analysis.

claim: Searching for HBsAg peptide-specific clonotypes in the memory repertoires prior to vaccination (day 0) results in a Rhbs with a significant difference between early- and late-converters (one-sided Wilcoxon-test p-value = 0.0010).
source: Furthermore, searching for HBsAg peptide-specific clonotypes in the memory repertoires prior to vaccination (day 0) results in a Rhbs with a similar difference (one-sided Wilcoxon-test p-value = 0.0010, Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 3D and statistical analysis.

claim: The presence of HBsAg peptide-specific clonotypes as defined by the ratio Rhbs can be used as a classifier to distinguish early- from late-converters prior to vaccination with an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.825 (95% CI: 0.657–0.994).
source: In this manner, the presence of HBsAg peptide-specific clonotypes as defined by the ratio Rhbs can be used as a classifier to distinguish early- from late-converters prior to vaccination (Figure 3E), with an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.825 (95% CI: 0.657–0.994) in a leave-one-out cross-validation setting.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: A significant increase in the frequency of vaccine-specific CD40L+4-1BB− memory CD4 T cells at day 60 was detected in the cohort.
source: We detected a significant increase in the frequency of vaccine-specific CD40L+4-1BB− and CD40L−4-1BB+ memory CD4 T cells at day 60 in our cohort (Figure 4A)
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: A significant increase in the frequency of vaccine-specific CD40L−4-1BB+ memory CD4 T cells at day 60 was detected in the cohort.
source: We detected a significant increase in the frequency of vaccine-specific CD40L+4-1BB− and CD40L−4-1BB+ memory CD4 T cells at day 60 in our cohort (Figure 4A)
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The frequency of vaccine-specific CD40L+4-1BB− memory CD4 T cells at day 60 correlated positively with the increase in antibody titer between day 0 and day 365.
source: that correlated positively with the increase in antibody titer between day 0 and day 365 (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: The frequency of vaccine-specific CD40L−4-1BB+ memory CD4 T cells at day 60 correlated positively with the increase in antibody titer between day 0 and day 365.
source: that correlated positively with the increase in antibody titer between day 0 and day 365 (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: The induction of both signatures of vaccine-specific memory CD4 T cells was only true for early-converters.
source: Upon a closer look, the induction of both signatures of vaccine-specific memory CD4 T cells was only true for early-converters (Figure 4C, see Figure 4—figure supplement 4A for non-converters and Figure 4—figure supplement 4B for vaccine-specific CD4 T cells).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 4A.

claim: Late-converters did not show a detectable memory CD4 T cell response.
source: Late-converters did not show a detectable memory CD4 T cell response.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: No significant differences in the frequencies of CD40L+4-1BB− memory CD4 T cells between early- and late-converters at day 0 were observed.
source: Although a subset of both early- and late-converters had detectable memory CD4 T cell responses prior to vaccination, we observed no significant differences in the frequencies of CD40L+4-1BB− and CD40L−4-1BB+ memory CD4 T cells between the two groups at day 0 (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: No significant differences in the frequencies of CD40L−4-1BB+ memory CD4 T cells between early- and late-converters at day 0 were observed.
source: Although a subset of both early- and late-converters had detectable memory CD4 T cell responses prior to vaccination, we observed no significant differences in the frequencies of CD40L+4-1BB− and CD40L−4-1BB+ memory CD4 T cells between the two groups at day 0 (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The Rhbs metric is a good predictor for HBsAg-specific memory CD4 T cells with a TCON signature identified at day 60 post-vaccination.
source: Results indicate that the Rhbs metric is a good predictor for HBsAg-specific memory CD4 T cells with a TCON signature (but not TREG signature) identified at day 60 post-vaccination (Figure 4E and F).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The Rhbs metric is not a good predictor for HBsAg-specific memory CD4 T cells with a TREG signature identified at day 60 post-vaccination.
source: Results indicate that the Rhbs metric is a good predictor for HBsAg-specific memory CD4 T cells with a TCON signature (but not TREG signature) identified at day 60 post-vaccination (Figure 4E and F).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The classifier is less performant for the prediction of CD4 T cell response at later time points (days 180 and 365).
source: However, the classifier is less performant for the prediction of CD4 T cell response at later time points.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 4E and F.

claim: A significantly higher frequency of 4-1BB+ CD45RA− TREG cells in late-converters compared to early-converters was identified.
source: Using manual gating in which regulatory T cells (TREG) were defined as viable CD3+CD4+CD8−CD25+CD127−CXCR5− and were further divided into CD45RA+ and CD45RA− TREG cells, we identified a significantly higher frequency of 4-1BB+ CD45RA− TREG cells in late-converters compared to early-converters (Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: TREG cells showed higher 4-1BB expression compared to TH, cTFH, and cTFR cells.
source: TREG cells showed higher 4-1BB expression compared to TH, cTFH, and cTFR cells (Figure 5B)
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Within TREG subset, CD45RA− TREG cells showed significantly higher expression of 4-1BB compared to CD45RA+ TREG cells.
source: and within TREG subset, CD45RA− TREG cells showed significantly higher expression of 4-1BB, accompanied with a higher expression of CD25, compared to CD45RA+ TREG cells (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: CD45RA− TREG cells showed higher expression of CD25 compared to CD45RA+ TREG cells.
source: and within TREG subset, CD45RA− TREG cells showed significantly higher expression of 4-1BB, accompanied with a higher expression of CD25, compared to CD45RA+ TREG cells (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: No differences were detected in the frequency of CD45RA− or CD45RA+ TREG cells within CD4 T cell compartment between early- and late-converters.
source: It is worth noting here that no differences were detected in the frequency of CD45RA− or CD45RA+ TREG cells within CD4 T cell compartment between the two groups (Figure 5D)
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: It is the composition of TREG compartment that is distinct between early- and late-converters.
source: and that it is the composition of TREG compartment that is distinct between the two groups (Figure 5E).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: An expanded subset of 4-1BB+CD45RA− TREG cells pre-vaccination is a prominent feature of a delayed and modest immune response to HB vaccine in the cohort.
source: In summary, an expanded subset of 4-1BB+CD45RA− TREG cells pre-vaccination is a prominent feature of a delayed and modest immune response to HB vaccine in our cohort.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 5A and related analyses.

claim: Preexisting memory CD4 T cell TCRβ sequences specific to HBsAg predict which individuals will mount an early and more vigorous immune response to the vaccine as evidenced by a higher fold change in anti-HBs antibody titer.
source: Our systems immunology data supports the theory that preexisting memory CD4 T cell TCRβ sequences specific to HBsAg, the antigenic component of the current HB vaccine, predict which individuals will mount an early and more vigorous immune response to the vaccine as evidenced by a higher fold change in anti-HBs antibody titer and a more significant induction of antigen-specific CD4 T cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Preexisting memory CD4 T cell TCRβ sequences specific to HBsAg predict which individuals will mount an early and more vigorous immune response to the vaccine as evidenced by a more significant induction of antigen-specific CD4 T cells.
source: Our systems immunology data supports the theory that preexisting memory CD4 T cell TCRβ sequences specific to HBsAg, the antigenic component of the current HB vaccine, predict which individuals will mount an early and more vigorous immune response to the vaccine as evidenced by a higher fold change in anti-HBs antibody titer and a more significant induction of antigen-specific CD4 T cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Preexisting memory CD4 T cell clonotypes are generated due to the highly degenerate nature of T cell recognition of antigen/MHC and are cross-reactive to environmental antigens.
source: It is postulated that preexisting memory CD4 T cell clonotypes are generated due to the highly degenerate nature of T cell recognition of antigen/MHC and are cross-reactive to environmental antigens (Sewell, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Sewell, 2012.

claim: Preexisting memory CD4 T cells are well-established in unexposed HIV-seronegative individuals, although at a significantly lower magnitude than HIV-exposed seronegative individuals.
source: For example, preexisting memory CD4 T cells are well-established in unexposed HIV-seronegative individuals, although at a significantly lower magnitude than HIV-exposed seronegative individuals (Campion et al., 2014; Ritchie et al., 2011)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Campion et al., 2014 and Ritchie et al., 2011.

claim: Preexisting memory CD4 T cells in HIV-seronegative individuals were likely primed by exposure to environmental triggers or the human microbiome.
source: and were likely primed by exposure to environmental triggers or the human microbiome.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the origin of preexisting memory CD4 T cells.

claim: The TCRβ repertoire of CD4 T cells encodes the antigen exposure history of each individual.
source: We and others have shown before that the TCRβ repertoire of CD4 T cells encodes the antigen exposure history of each individual and that antigen-specific TCRβ sequences could serve to automatically annotate the infection or exposure history (DeWitt et al., 2018; Emerson et al., 2017; De Neuter et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to DeWitt et al., 2018; Emerson et al., 2017; De Neuter et al., 2019.

claim: Antigen-specific TCRβ sequences could serve to automatically annotate the infection or exposure history.
source: We and others have shown before that the TCRβ repertoire of CD4 T cells encodes the antigen exposure history of each individual and that antigen-specific TCRβ sequences could serve to automatically annotate the infection or exposure history (DeWitt et al., 2018; Emerson et al., 2017; De Neuter et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to DeWitt et al., 2018; Emerson et al., 2017; De Neuter et al., 2019.

claim: The recruitment of novel vaccine-specific T cell clonotypes into memory compartment following vaccination can be tracked by examining the CD4 memory TCRβ repertoire over time.
source: Specifically, the recruitment of novel vaccine-specific T cell clonotypes into memory compartment following vaccination can be tracked by examining the CD4 memory TCRβ repertoire over time.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: No increase in the frequency of the vaccine-specific memory T cells was observed.
source: While we observed no increase in the frequency of the vaccine-specific memory T cells, as the time point may have missed the peak of the clonal expansion of effector CD4 T cells as was reported before (Blom et al., 2013; Kohler et al., 2012; Pogorelyy et al., 2018)
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E and citations to Blom et al., 2013; Kohler et al., 2012; Pogorelyy et al., 2018.

claim: A significant rise in the number of unique vaccine-specific T cell clonotypes was detected.
source: a significant rise in the number of unique vaccine-specific T cell clonotypes was detected.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Antigen-specific TCRβ sequences do not always overlap with those sequences that increase in frequency after infection or vaccination.
source: This observation is consistent with earlier studies of T cell immune repertoire that showed that antigen-specific TCRβ sequences do not always overlap with those sequences that increase in frequency after infection or vaccination (DeWitt et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to DeWitt et al., 2015.

claim: Individuals with the earlier and more robust response against the vaccine had a telltale antigen-specific signature in their memory TCRβ repertoire prior to vaccination.
source: More interestingly, individuals with the earlier and more robust response against the vaccine had a telltale antigen-specific signature in their memory TCRβ repertoire prior to vaccination, despite the lack of HBsAg antibodies and prior vaccination history.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: CD40L+4-1BB− CD4 T cells have a CD25lowCD127high phenotype.
source: Using the converse expression of CD40L and 4-1BB, CD40L+4-1BB− and CD40L−4-1BB+ CD4 T cells have a CD25lowCD127high and CD25highCD127low phenotype, respectively (Figure 4—figure supplement 2)

claim: CD40L−4-1BB+ CD4 T cells have a CD25highCD127low phenotype.
source: Using the converse expression of CD40L and 4-1BB, CD40L+4-1BB− and CD40L−4-1BB+ CD4 T cells have a CD25lowCD127high and CD25highCD127low phenotype, respectively (Figure 4—figure supplement 2)
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: The converse expression of CD40L and 4-1BB validates their use for the distinction of activated TCON and TREG cells.
source: and validate their use for the distinction of activated TCON and TREG cells as described before (Schoenbrunn et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2 and citation to Schoenbrunn et al., 2012.

claim: Commercially available HBV vaccines produce a robust and long-lasting anti-HBs response.
source: Commercially available HBV vaccines produce a robust and long-lasting anti-HBs response, and protection is provided by induction of an anti-HBs (antibody against HBV surface antigen) titer higher than 10 mIU/ml after a complete immunization schedule of three doses (Meireles et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Meireles et al., 2015.

claim: 5–10% of healthy adult vaccinees fail to produce protective titers of anti-HBs and can be classified as non-responders.
source: However, 5–10% of healthy adult vaccinees fail to produce protective titers of anti-HBs and can be classified as non-responders (Meireles et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Meireles et al., 2015.

claim: In the cohort, 13 vaccinees did not seroconvert by day 60.
source: In our cohort, 13 vaccinees did not seroconvert by day 60 (30 days following administration of the second vaccine dose), as determined by antibody titer.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data presented in the manuscript.

claim: TREG cells represent about 5–10% of human CD4 T cell compartment.
source: TREG cells represent about 5–10% of human CD4 T cell compartment and are identified by the constitutive surface expression of CD25, also known as IL-2 receptor α subunit (IL-2Ra), and the nuclear expression of forkhead family transcription factor 3 (Foxp3), a lineage specification factor of TREG cells (Rudensky, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Rudensky, 2011.

claim: TREG cells are identified by the constitutive surface expression of CD25 and the nuclear expression of Foxp3.
source: TREG cells represent about 5–10% of human CD4 T cell compartment and are identified by the constitutive surface expression of CD25, also known as IL-2 receptor α subunit (IL-2Ra), and the nuclear expression of forkhead family transcription factor 3 (Foxp3), a lineage specification factor of TREG cells (Rudensky, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Rudensky, 2011.

claim: Foxp3 is a lineage specification factor of TREG cells.
source: TREG cells represent about 5–10% of human CD4 T cell compartment and are identified by the constitutive surface expression of CD25, also known as IL-2 receptor α subunit (IL-2Ra), and the nuclear expression of forkhead family transcription factor 3 (Foxp3), a lineage specification factor of TREG cells (Rudensky, 2011).
